title: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax — blebs & management
clinicalHistory: 20-year-old male, tall and thin, sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. No trauma. SpO₂ 94% on room air.
technique: Contrast-enhanced CT chest (diagnostic) + prior PA chest radiograph when available.
primaryDiagnosis: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with apical blebs
learningObjectives: Recognise visceral pleural line and absent peripheral lung markings.
Identify apical blebs on CT as the usual mechanism in primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Describe safe pleural drain insertion (triangle of safety / 2nd ICS MCL) and when to escalate.
discussion: Teaching narrative synthesised from open Radiopaedia case discussions (primary spontaneous pneumothorax, apical blebs). Imaging in this catalog entry uses the public FlowRad/Pacsbin demo CT until a dedicated de-identified study is ingested to Orthanc.
references: Radiopaedia — Pneumothorax case discussion & drain MCQ (https://radiopaedia.org/cases/pneumothorax-61)

findings.label: Pneumothorax — visceral pleural line
findings.description: A thin white visceral pleural line separates aerated lung from pleural gas. Peripheral lung markings disappear beyond the line.
teachingPoints: On erect imaging, gas rises — scrutinise the apex first.
Do not mistake skin folds or medial lung for a pleural line.

findings.label: Apical blebs
findings.description: CT through the lung apices shows subpleural blebs — the usual rupture site in primary spontaneous pneumothorax in young males.
teachingPoints: Scroll the apices on lung and bone windows.
Bilateral blebs increase recurrence risk — document them.

findings.label: Drain planning
findings.description: Small-bore pigtail via the triangle of safety (or 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line for tension). Tip directed toward the apex.
teachingPoints: Tension physiology needs immediate decompression — do not wait for CT.
Re-expansion pulmonary oedema is rare but life-threatening — watch fluid status.
